Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "At the Bellweather Playhouse, the lighting crew was small enough that everyone knew which drawer held the spare fuses, but the room still felt busy during the week before opening. Mara, the lighting supervisor, worked with Eli at the board and Jun, who handled the ladders and cables. Their production of The Glass Orchard had a narrow set, a painted orchard wall, and a single blue door that needed to look like different places as the story moved from morning to night. The crew had been in the building since Monday, and by Wednesday they were trying to finish focus, repair a stubborn work light, and leave the stage clear for the actors’ evening rehearsal.

Mara began each shift by checking the paper plot against the fixtures overhead. The plot had been revised after the director moved a bench and asked for more light on the actors’ faces, so Mara marked the change in pencil rather than covering the old note with tape. Eli checked the console file and confirmed that the house lights, work lights, and show cues were saved in separate places. Jun walked the cable paths with a coil of black tape, making sure no line crossed the entrance the actors used. They did not rush through those checks, even when the front desk called to ask when the stage would be free.

1. Before the house opens

On Thursday afternoon, the three of them tested the opening sequence without the actors. A warm wash came up over the orchard wall, then a narrow special found the blue door as the rest of the stage faded. The change looked smooth from the middle seats, but from the left aisle Mara could see a pale patch on the painted floor. Jun shifted the angle of one fixture, and Eli adjusted the cue so the fade took a little longer. They ran it again from the back row, where the door seemed too bright, then agreed on a smaller level change instead of moving the fixture a second time.

The dimmer rack made a clicking sound whenever one channel rose above half. It had made the same noise during the previous show, and the venue manager had asked the crew to keep a note of when it happened. Eli tested the channel with a work light, then tried a different circuit. The click disappeared, but that circuit was already carrying the practical lamp in the set. Mara wrote both observations on the maintenance sheet and asked the manager to look at the rack before the next rental. For the evening rehearsal, they kept the original channel below the level where the noise started.

During a break, Jun found a loose screw in the clamp above the stage-left window. He brought down the ladder and held it while Mara checked the fixture, then replaced the screw with one from the crew’s small hardware tin. The tin had washers, bolts, a few cable ties, and a label that had faded until only the word “lighting” was clear. Eli stayed at the board and watched the stage while they worked. Once the fixture was secured, Mara gave it a light tug and checked that its safety cable was still attached. Jun returned the ladder to the marked storage spot instead of leaning it against the wall.

The director arrived early and watched the lighting changes from the first row. She asked whether the orchard could feel colder when the main character returned to the door, but she did not want the actors’ skin tones to turn blue. Mara tried a cooler color from the side fixtures while leaving the front light warm. The director watched the scene, waited a moment, and said, “That keeps the room chilly without making the people look ill.” Eli saved the look as a separate cue so it could be compared with the earlier version. They left both versions in the file until the next rehearsal, when the actors would be in place.

By Friday, the crew had a practical order for finishing the work. Jun checked the clamps and safety cables from the floor while Mara followed the plot overhead, calling out fixture numbers. Eli listened from the board and marked each fixture as they confirmed its focus. They paused whenever an actor or stage manager needed to cross the room, and they put the ladder away before the doors opened. A fresh roll of tape went into the workbox, along with the maintenance sheet and a small flashlight. The crew also left a clear aisle between the console and the exit, where a stack of scenery had briefly narrowed the path.

The first full run did not go exactly as planned. One cue came in late because Eli was watching the actors’ movement rather than the stage manager’s hand, and the next cue revealed a strip of unpainted wood beside the door. Nobody stopped the run. Mara wrote down the timing change, and Jun covered the bright strip with a temporary piece of painted cloth after the actors had left. They checked the view from several seats before deciding it was hidden well enough for the weekend. The stage manager added the cue adjustment to the rehearsal notes, so Eli could try it at the next run without changing the saved version used for that night.

At the end of the shift, Mara copied the final fixture notes into the crew binder. She recorded which channel clicked, which alternate circuit they had tested, and the level they used during rehearsal. Eli made a backup of the console file on the theatre’s labeled drive and checked that the cue names matched the paper plot. Jun returned the hardware tin, tape, and flashlight to their usual shelves. They did not call the work finished; the actors still had another rehearsal, and the manager had not yet inspected the dimmer rack. Before leaving, Mara switched off the work lights one row at a time and checked the stage from the lobby door.

The next morning, the building was scheduled to host a children’s dance class before the play’s matinee. The crew left the floor free of cable and moved the loose scenery pieces to the marked storage area. Mara put a note on the lighting desk asking the class leader not to use the stage-left wall outlet, which shared a circuit with the work light. The note also gave the venue manager’s extension in case the room needed attention. Outside, rain had started to collect along the pavement, so Jun placed a mat inside the loading entrance to keep wet footprints away from the cables.
